title: The amoraim
hook: the sages of the Gemara, who discussed the Mishnah for three centuries

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tanna, a teacher of the Mishnah, and Rabbi Meir, who lit up the sages' eyes. Your line: the teachers of the mishnah. Today, the ones who explained them.

A sage is bathing in the Jordan River. A rough stranger sees him from the bank and, in one leap, jumps into the water after him. The sage is Rabbi Yochanan. The stranger is a man the Talmud calls Resh Lakish, and the story says he had been living as a robber. Rabbi Yochanan says: your strength should be for Torah. Resh Lakish answers: your beauty should be for women. They strike a deal: if he'll turn to study, Rabbi Yochanan will give him his sister in marriage. He does. And the robber becomes a sage whose words fill the Talmud.
screen: `A LEAP INTO THE JORDAN.` → `YOUR STRENGTH FOR TORAH.` → `THE ROBBER BECOMES A SAGE.`

segments.voice: Amora. In the plural, amoraim. The tannaim gave the Mishnah its words. The amoraim are the sages who came after, in the land of Israel and in Babylonia, and spent generations discussing those words line by line. Their discussion is the Gemara. Mishnah plus Gemara: the Talmud. The word is Aramaic, and Jastrow's dictionary ties it to the verb to say: a speaker, an expounder. A few pairs to know: Rav and Shmuel in Babylonia, Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish in the land of Israel, and later Abaye and Rava. They're remembered in pairs. Explaining was done with someone. Back to the riverbank, in tractate Bava Metzia. Years later, after a bitter quarrel, Resh Lakish dies, and Rabbi Yochanan is crushed. The sages send him a brilliant student, Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat. Whatever Rabbi Yochanan says, Rabbi Elazar answers: there's a teaching that supports you. Rabbi Yochanan can't bear it. In paraphrase: are you like the son of Lakish? When I said something, he raised twenty-four objections, I gave twenty-four answers, and the matter came clear on its own. You only tell me I'm right. I know I'm right. The story ends in grief, with Rabbi Yochanan crying out for his friend. For the amoraim, explaining wasn't agreeing. It was pushing back, hard, until the teaching came clear.
screen: `AFTER THE TANNAIM, THE AMORAIM.` · `AMORA: ONE WHO SAYS, WHO EXPOUNDS.` · `RAV AND SHMUEL; ABAYE AND RAVA.` · `TWENTY-FOUR OBJECTIONS, AND IT CAME CLEAR.` · then, large: `THE EXPLAINERS.`

segments.voice: Say the name Resh Lakish quietly a few times, the man who leapt into the river, until it stays. Then bring to mind someone who pushes back on you in a way that leaves you clearer instead of smaller, and hold their face for a while. If you pray, you can give thanks for them; if not, just notice what they've given you.
Amora. One of the sages of the Gemara, who discussed the Mishnah line by line, tied in the dictionary to the verb to say. Today's word.
Your line: the explainers. A friend who pushes back can leave you clearer, not smaller. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Talmud study is traditionally done in pairs, a chavruta, where two learners read aloud, question each other and argue their way to the meaning of a passage.

chat.says: My study partner argues with everything I say. Isn't that bad for learning?
options: Not in the Talmud: Resh Lakish raised twenty-four objections, and the teaching came clear.
Yes. The amoraim taught that a good partner agrees, so the teaching stays calm.
Yes. Rabbi Yochanan was glad when Rabbi Elazar simply agreed with him.
chat.meaning: Rabbi Yochanan missed Resh Lakish's objections. For the amoraim, explaining meant pushing back until the teaching came clear.

notes: Bava Metzia 84a paraphrased: Resh Lakish leaps into the Jordan after Rabbi Yochanan; 'your strength for Torah' / 'your beauty for women'; Yochanan offers his sister; Resh Lakish's death after a quarrel; Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat's 'there is a baraita that supports you'; 'twenty-four objections ... twenty-four answers'; Yochanan's grief. The number twenty-four is the text's own. 'Had been living as a robber' renders the Talmud's description of him as a bandit (some readers say a gladiator). Please confirm.

The quarrel (over when knives and weapons become susceptible to impurity) is mentioned only as 'a bitter quarrel'; the story's darker ending (Yochanan losing his mind with grief, the sages praying for his death) is softened to 'the story ends in grief'. Please confirm this is acceptable.
Amora tied to 'say, expound' via Jastrow (cited). The amora was also the speaker who relayed a teacher's lecture aloud; not mentioned. Please confirm.
Pairs named (Rav and Shmuel; Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish; Abaye and Rava) without dates. The outline's 'three centuries' is not stated, under the claims rule.
